An intranet serves internal users only, an extranet gives named partners controlled access to shared resources, and a guest network gives visitors internet access without reaching company systems.

question: A company expects to hire the same IT consultancy for many projects over several years. Which agreement should it negotiate once to set the legal and payment terms that each later project will follow?
explanation: A master service agreement (MSA) sets the standing legal and commercial terms for an ongoing relationship, so each new project needs only a short statement of work instead of a new contract. A statement of work (SOW) defines one project's tasks and deliverables, a memorandum of understanding (MOU) records nonbinding intent, and a service level agreement (SLA) sets performance targets such as uptime.

question: When a company opened its cloud account, an administrator wrote an IAM policy giving every virtual machine full administrative rights over all storage buckets, and the policy has not changed since. Only two machines need to read one bucket. Which type of vulnerability does this policy create?
explanation: A misconfiguration is a setting that leaves a system less secure than it should be, and a cloud policy that grants far more access than is needed is among the most common examples. Privilege creep is the gradual build-up of rights as a person changes roles, whereas this policy was too broad from the first day and has stayed the same. Resource reuse concerns leftover data on shared hardware, and a supply chain vulnerability comes from a supplier's product or service.

question: A code review finds that a web application builds each SQL command by joining fixed text with whatever a visitor types into a search box. Which defense stops the typed text from being run as part of the command?
explanation: A parameterized query sends the SQL command and the user's value to the database separately, so the value is always treated as data and never as code. Output encoding stops injected script from running in a browser, anti-forgery tokens stop forged requests that start on another site, and secure cookie flags protect the session cookie. None of them changes how the database reads the input.

question: One workstation renames thousands of files on a shared drive to a new extension within minutes, and staff can no longer open them. Just before, a process on it deleted the Windows volume shadow copies. Which type of malware do these indicators point to?
explanation: Ransomware encrypts files so that they can no longer be opened, often after deleting the volume shadow copies that could restore them. Mass renaming of files to one new extension is another common sign. A virus attaches its code to other files and spreads when they are run, a worm copies itself across a network on its own, and a rootkit hides malware from the operating system instead of locking data away.

question: A developer commits updated code to a central repository. The repository records who made each modification, what was altered and when, and it can return any file to an earlier state. Which technology provides these features?
explanation: Version control keeps every revision of a file with its author and time, which gives an audit trail of modifications and a way back to any earlier state. Continuous integration builds and tests each commit automatically, static code analysis searches source code for flaws, and file integrity monitoring reports unexpected alterations to files on a running system.

question: In a company's internal PKI, a user's certificate was signed by Intermediate CA 2, whose certificate was signed by Intermediate CA 1, whose certificate was signed by the root CA. What is this arrangement called?
explanation: A chain of trust runs from an end-entity certificate through each intermediate CA to a root CA that the client already trusts, and each certificate in it is signed by the one above. Cross-certification links two separate CA hierarchies by having their CAs certify each other. Certificate pinning makes an application accept only one expected certificate or key. Trust on first use, as in SSH, accepts a key the first time it is seen and remembers it.

question: A security review finds that an online store keeps customers' card numbers in plaintext in its database. The store must read the full numbers again to bill repeat orders. Which change BEST protects the stored numbers under PCI DSS?
options: Mask the numbers and log each time one is shown
Encrypt the numbers and restrict access to the keys
Isolate the numbers and filter traffic to their segment
Hash the numbers and store the digests in their place
explanation: PCI DSS requires stored card numbers to be unreadable, and strong encryption with tightly controlled keys is a method that still lets an authorized system recover them. A hash cannot be reversed, so the store could not bill repeat orders. Masking changes what is displayed and leaves the stored plaintext as it is, and isolating the numbers on their own network segment narrows who can reach them without making them unreadable.

question: Technicians from an IT services contractor will receive accounts on a company's network to provide routine support. Which document should each technician sign to agree to what is permitted and forbidden on the company's systems?
explanation: An acceptable use policy (AUP) sets out what users may and may not do with an organization's systems, and contractors who receive accounts should sign it just as employees do. A non-disclosure agreement protects confidential information rather than governing system use, a service level agreement sets the contractor's performance targets, and rules of engagement govern a security test, not routine support work.

question: A change review finds that a middleware update will make the order system unavailable to customers for about 30 minutes while several services reload. Which technical implication of the change does the team need to schedule and announce?
explanation: Downtime is the period in which a change makes a service unavailable, so it is planned for a maintenance window and announced to the people it affects. Legacy applications are the implication when an older program cannot work with the new version. Allow lists matter when changed software must be approved again before it can run. Restricted activities are actions that fall outside the approved scope of the change.

question: A group with no connection to a mining company breaks into its mail server, copies emails that show safety violations and sends them to journalists. The group asks for no money. Which threat actor type does this describe?
explanation: A hacktivist attacks to draw public attention to a cause, which is why the stolen material goes to the press and no payment is sought. Organized crime would sell the emails or demand money for them. An insider threat is someone with authorized access, and this group has no connection to the company. Shadow IT is staff using unapproved technology for their work.

question: A monitoring tool shows one workstation sending connection attempts to every TCP port, from 1 to 65,535, on each host in its subnet. Which activity does this pattern indicate?
explanation: A sweep of every port on every host is reconnaissance: the source is mapping which hosts and services exist before it attacks them. Data exfiltration appears as large transfers to an outside address. Lateral movement appears as logons or remote sessions from one internal host to another. A denial of service appears as a flood aimed at one target to exhaust it.

question: A flat network puts 800 workstations, 40 servers, the printers and the IP cameras in one broadcast domain. The team wants a compromised workstation to be unable to reach the cameras and to reach servers only on approved ports. Which design achieves this?
options: Separate VLANs joined by a filtering firewall
Address translation between the device groups
An intrusion prevention system at the network core
explanation: Putting each device group in its own VLAN and routing between the VLANs through a firewall forces every cross-group connection past rules that allow only approved flows. An intrusion prevention system blocks known attack patterns rather than limiting which hosts may talk, address translation changes addresses without blocking anything, and 802.1X on its own decides which devices may join the network but does not limit them afterward.

question: A Linux web server must be hardened so that, even if an attacker takes over the web server process, it can reach only the files and ports that a central policy allows, regardless of ordinary file permissions. Which control should be enabled?
explanation: SELinux enforces mandatory access control, confining a process to the files and ports its policy allows even when the account it runs under has wider ordinary permissions. An iptables firewall filters network traffic but not file access, file permissions are discretionary and follow the user rather than a central policy, and sudo rules limit which commands users may run with raised privileges. AppArmor, the default on Ubuntu, gives similar confinement.

question: After a breach investigation closes, the lead examiner writes a document setting out the evidence collected, the tools and methods used and the conclusions drawn, for management and the company's lawyers. Which forensic activity is this?
explanation: Reporting is the forensic step that documents what was examined, how it was examined and what was found, in a form that managers, lawyers and courts can rely on. Preservation keeps evidence unchanged, e-discovery finds electronic records and hands them to the other side in a legal case, and a legal hold stops relevant data from being deleted.

question: A bank's mobile app reads each phone's GPS position and refuses to display account records when the phone is outside the country. Which method of securing data does the app apply?
explanation: Geographic restrictions allow or refuse access to data according to where the user or device is, as found from GPS, the wireless network or the IP address. Permission restrictions depend on who the user is and not on where, segmentation separates data into different stores or network zones, and obfuscation disguises data to make it hard to understand.

question: After a web application firewall is deployed, the risk analyst lowers the ARO for SQL injection in the risk register. What change in the threat does that record?
options: Each attack would expose a smaller share of the data
Successful attacks are expected less frequently
Recovery after each attack is expected to be faster
Each successful attack would cost less to clean up
explanation: The annualized rate of occurrence is how often a loss event is expected in a year, so a control that blocks most attacks lowers it while the cost of each attack stays the same. A lower cost per attack would change the single loss expectancy, a smaller share of data exposed would change the exposure factor, and faster recovery would show in the mean time to repair.

question: A cloud application lets a user open payroll records only when the user works in finance, the device passes its compliance check and the request arrives during business hours. Which access control model does this describe?
explanation: Attribute-based access control decides each request from attributes of the user, the device, the resource and the environment, such as department, compliance state and time. Role-based access control grants rights through job roles alone, mandatory access control compares labels with clearances, and discretionary access control leaves the decision to each resource owner.

question: Staff working on an unannounced product are told not to discuss it on flights or in restaurants and not to mention it in social media posts. Which training topic does this guidance come from?
explanation: Operational security trains staff to keep details of sensitive work out of public conversations and social media, where an adversary could collect and combine them. Situational awareness is about noticing suspicious people and objects nearby, remote work training covers working safely outside the office, and insider threat training covers spotting colleagues who misuse their access.

question: A remote access server checks each user's password, applies the permissions assigned to the user's group, and logs the start and end of every session. Which security concept describes this set of functions?
explanation: AAA stands for authentication, authorization and accounting: proving who a user is, deciding what the user may do, and recording what the user did. The CIA triad names the goals of confidentiality, integrity and availability, zero trust verifies every request wherever it comes from, and defense in depth layers several controls.

question: After a company is found to have sold surveillance software to a government under an international embargo, its own government bars banks and suppliers at home from doing business with it. Which consequence of non-compliance is this?
explanation: Sanctions are penalties or restrictions that a government imposes, such as a ban on trading with a company, and they can cut a business off from its banks and suppliers. Loss of license removes a regulator's permission to operate, reputational damage is a loss of trust among customers and the public, and contractual impacts come from the terms of agreements with partners.

question: An emailed link points to a real shopping site, and its search parameter contains a script. The results page prints the search text back unchanged, so the script runs in the browser of anyone who follows the link. Nothing is saved on the site. Which vulnerability does this show?
explanation: Reflected cross-site scripting sends a script to the site inside a request, and the site returns it in the immediate response, so it reaches only users who follow the crafted link. Persistent (stored) cross-site scripting keeps the script on the site for every later visitor. Cross-site request forgery makes the victim's browser perform an action without running an injected script, and server-side request forgery makes the application itself fetch an address.

question: An attacker replaces the home page of an oil company's website with a statement calling for a ban on offshore drilling. The rest of the site keeps working and no data is taken. Which motivation BEST describes this attack?
explanation: A defacement that carries a message is driven by philosophical or political beliefs, because its purpose is to make a statement in public. Service disruption is ruled out because the rest of the site keeps working. Financial gain would bring a demand for payment, and espionage depends on taking information quietly, which a public defacement does not do.

question: An attacker on a Windows server set up a script to run every night at 3 AM, even after restarts. Which log would record when this was set up?
explanation: Windows records each new scheduled task as event 106, task registered, in the Task Scheduler operational log when task history is on, which makes that log the place to look for persistence that runs at a set time. The Security log can also record it, as event 4698, when object access auditing is on. The BITS Client log records background transfer jobs, which attackers also abuse but which do not run on a clock, the DNS Client log records name lookups, and the Print Service log records print jobs.

question: A playbook blocks at the firewall each address that appears in a threat intelligence feed. The feed lists a business partner's address by mistake, and the partner is cut off for six hours until someone notices. Which risk of automation does this show?
options: It adds complexity that makes the workflow hard to maintain
It acts on faulty input before a person has checked the action
It builds up technical debt that is costly to remove later
It becomes a single point of failure for the security team
explanation: Automation carries out its instructions at machine speed, so a wrong entry in its input is enforced before any person can question it. An allow list of partner addresses or an approval step for blocking actions reduces that risk. A single point of failure would mean that blocking stopped when the playbook itself failed. Technical debt and complexity are costs of building and maintaining automation, not of acting on bad data.

question: Logon records show an intruder using one stolen account on an HR workstation, then connecting from it to a manager's laptop, from there to a print server and finally to a file server. Which technique does this progression indicate?
explanation: Lateral movement is an intruder's progress from one compromised host to the next inside a network, usually toward more valuable systems. Privilege escalation would show the account gaining rights it did not have, but the same account is used throughout. Data exfiltration would show files leaving the network. Persistence would show a change that keeps access after a restart, such as a new scheduled task.

question: In a large company, each business unit sets its own security priorities, budget and controls, with little direction from the center. Which weakness does this structure typically bring?
options: Long delays while many groups reach agreement
Slow responses to each unit's local needs
Safeguards that differ from unit to unit
Oversight that sits far from daily operations
explanation: Decentralized governance lets each unit move quickly on its own needs, but security controls and their strength then vary from one unit to the next. Slow responses to local needs are the usual cost of centralized governance, long delays while groups agree are the cost of committee decisions, and distance from daily operations is a limit of oversight by a board.

question: An email's link text shows the address of the company's payroll site. Which check lets an employee see the address the link will actually open, without clicking it?
options: Reading the sender's full email address
Hovering the pointer over the link
explanation: Hovering the pointer over a link shows the real destination address, which in a phishing email often differs from the text on display. The sender's address reveals a lookalike sending domain, the message headers show which servers handled the message, and a padlock shows only that a page already opened uses an encrypted connection.

question: A vendor collected a company's old hard drives and shredded them off site. An auditor now asks for evidence that each drive, listed by serial number, was shredded. Which document should the company provide?
explanation: A certificate of destruction is the vendor's signed statement that named media, often listed by serial number, was destroyed, and it gives the company evidence for its auditors. Chain of custody documents show who held the drives and when, the sanitization policy sets how media must be handled, and the service contract states what the vendor promised, but none of them shows that the shredding was done.

question: Two identical web servers run as an active-active cluster, and one of them fails. What happens to the traffic it was serving?
options: It resumes once a spare is built from backup
The remaining node absorbs it on top of its own load
It moves to the DR site once failover is declared
An idle standby node is promoted to take it over
explanation: In an active-active cluster every node serves traffic at the same time, so when one fails the others absorb its share without waiting for anything to start. Promoting an idle standby describes an active-passive cluster, resuming once a spare is built from backup describes a cold spare, and moving to a DR site after failover is declared describes site-level recovery.

question: A new accounts clerk is given access to the two file shares and the billing application that the job requires, and to nothing else. Which principle does this apply?
explanation: Least privilege gives each account only the access its job requires, so that a mistake or a stolen login can reach as little as possible. Separation of duties splits a sensitive task between people, a mandatory vacation makes staff step away so that others can spot irregular work, and defense in depth layers several controls so that one failure is not enough.

question: A company keeps a register of every kind of personal data it holds, recording why it is collected, which systems store it and which teams use it. What is this register?
explanation: A data inventory records what personal data an organization holds, why it holds it, where it is stored and who uses it, and it supports the record of processing activities that GDPR requires. A retention schedule sets how long each type of record is kept, a data flow diagram shows how data moves between systems, and a classification policy defines sensitivity labels and how each must be handled.

question: A PowerShell command on a workstation downloaded a second-stage payload over unencrypted HTTP and ran it in memory, so nothing was written to disk. Which data source could still hold a copy of the payload?
explanation: Full packet capture records the contents of network traffic, so a payload fetched over unencrypted HTTP can be extracted from it even though nothing was written to disk. Firewall session logs and NetFlow records show which hosts talked, when and how much, and DNS query logs show which names were looked up, but none of them keeps the content itself.

question: Firewall logs show an outside address sending the first packet of the TCP handshake to each port on a server in turn. Whenever the server replies with the second packet, the outside address sends a reset instead of completing the handshake. Which type of scan is this?
explanation: A SYN scan sends only the first packet of the handshake and resets each connection that the target accepts, so it finds open ports without ever completing a connection. A connect scan completes the three-way handshake on every open port. An ACK scan sends acknowledgment packets alone, to learn which ports a firewall filters. The Xmas scan sets the FIN, PSH and URG flags and so never starts a handshake at all.

question: A change advisory board approves a request to edit an access control list on a core router. During the maintenance window, the edit blocks a port that the ERP application uses, and three offices lose access. The request never mentioned that port. Which part of the change process was incomplete?
explanation: An impact analysis identifies every system, port and user that a change will affect before it is approved, so a dependency it misses becomes an outage. The approval process worked as designed, because the board can judge only what the request shows. The maintenance window was used, and it limits when an outage happens, not whether it does. A post-implementation review comes afterward and records the lesson.

question: An EDR agent sees an unknown process try to read the memory of LSASS on a workstation and ends the process before any credentials are copied. In ending the process, which type of control did the EDR act as?
explanation: A preventive control stops a harmful action before it succeeds, such as ending a process before it can copy credentials from memory. A detective control records or reports an action for someone to act on, a deterrent control discourages an attacker from trying, and a compensating control stands in for a primary control that cannot be used.

question: Before an outside firm probes a vendor's systems for weaknesses, the firm and the vendor sign rules of engagement. What should this document define?
options: The deliverables, price and payment terms of the work
The uptime, response times and service credits owed
The methods allowed, the test hours and whom to call
The records, accounts and premises open to audit
explanation: Rules of engagement define how a security test may be carried out: which systems and techniques are in scope, when testing may take place and whom to contact if something goes wrong. A statement of work covers deliverables, price and payment terms; a service level agreement sets uptime, response times and service credits; and a right-to-audit clause says what the customer may examine.

question: A SIEM links four events on one workstation: a user opens an email attachment, PowerShell downloads a second program, that program adds itself to a registry Run key, and the workstation then probes other internal hosts. Which stage of the attack does the Run key represent?
explanation: A registry Run key starts a program at every logon, so adding one is persistence: it keeps the attacker's access after a restart. Initial access is the phishing attachment that the user opens. Execution is PowerShell running the downloaded code. Discovery is the probing of other internal hosts to learn what else can be reached.

question: A clinic must encrypt its laptops under a regulation, but a legacy application stops working on encrypted drives. Until the application is replaced, the laptops are kept in a badge-controlled room inside the building. Which control type is this arrangement?
explanation: A compensating control is an alternative measure that gives comparable protection when a required control cannot be put in place, and it is often temporary. A corrective control repairs or limits damage after an incident, a detective control identifies and records an incident, and a deterrent control discourages an attack without stopping it.

question: A policy requires disk encryption for confidential records held in the HR database and TLS for the same records when they are sent by email. Which concept explains why the same records need two different controls?
explanation: The control that fits a record depends on its state: disk encryption protects data at rest, TLS protects data in transit, and data in use needs protection in memory. The records keep one classification in every state, so classification does not explain the difference. Sovereignty concerns which country's laws apply, and retention concerns how long the records are kept.

question: After attackers stole data through a company's web application, the team works back through the web server logs and recent code changes to find the flaw that first let them in. Which activity is this?
explanation: Root cause analysis traces an incident back to the weakness that allowed it, such as the flaw that first let an attacker in, so that fixing it prevents a repeat. Threat hunting searches proactively for attackers who have not yet been detected, acquisition collects evidence such as logs and disk images, and eradication removes the attacker's malware and access.

question: A company invites outside researchers to test its public web services within published rules and pays for each valid flaw they report. What is this arrangement called?
explanation: A bug bounty program invites outside researchers to find and report flaws under published rules and rewards each valid report, usually with money. A penetration test and a red team engagement are carried out by contracted testers within an agreed scope and paid for by the engagement, and a threat intelligence feed supplies outside information about threats rather than reports of the company's own flaws.

question: A flaw is found in the code on a server's motherboard chip that starts the hardware before the operating system loads. An implant that abuses it survives a reinstall of the operating system and a replacement disk. At which layer does this vulnerability lie?
explanation: Firmware is the code stored on a device's own chips that starts the hardware, so a flaw there sits below the operating system and survives a reinstall or a new disk. An operating system flaw would be removed by a clean installation with current patches. A hypervisor is the layer that runs virtual machines, and an application flaw lives in a program installed on top of the operating system.

question: Employees leave Bluetooth switched on and discoverable so that their personal speakers pair with work laptops. An attacker in the parking lot connects to one laptop over Bluetooth and copies its contact list. Under which threat vector does CompTIA group this attack?
explanation: Bluetooth is a short-range radio link, and CompTIA lists it with wireless and wired connections under unsecure networks. A removable device is media such as a USB drive that is plugged into the computer. A message-based vector is email, SMS or instant messaging that carries a lure. A file-based vector is a document or program that runs harmful code when it is opened.

question: A company moves sign-in for all its applications from an internal directory to a cloud identity provider that users reach over the internet. Which attack can an outsider now aim at the sign-in service from anywhere?
explanation: An identity provider that is reachable from the internet invites password spraying, in which an attacker tries a few common passwords against many accounts from anywhere and stays under each account's lockout limit. Pass-the-hash needs password hashes taken from computers inside the network, shoulder surfing needs someone close enough to watch a user type, and a rogue access point needs someone within radio range. Multifactor authentication is the usual defense against spraying.

question: A SOC manager wants one screen that updates continuously and shows open alerts by severity, the hosts with the most failed sign-ins and the status of each open incident. Which data source fits this need?
explanation: A dashboard gathers live data from tools such as a SIEM into one continuously updated view, so it shows the current state of alerts, sign-ins and incidents at a glance. An automated report is a fixed summary produced on a schedule, a vulnerability scan lists weaknesses on hosts, and a packet capture records raw network traffic for detailed analysis.

question: Before showing the design drawings for a new product to three possible manufacturers, a company asks each one to sign an agreement not to reveal the drawings or use them for any other purpose. Which agreement is this?
explanation: A non-disclosure agreement (NDA) legally binds the signer to keep specified information confidential and to use it only for the stated purpose. A memorandum of understanding (MOU) records nonbinding intent to cooperate, a statement of work (SOW) defines the tasks of a project, and a business partners agreement (BPA) sets the terms of a partnership.

question: A visitor with no badge waits beside a door controlled by a badge reader. When an employee badges in, the visitor walks through behind the employee before the door closes. Which physical attack is this?
explanation: Tailgating is entering a secured area by following closely behind an authorized person, so that one valid badge lets two people in. RFID cloning copies a badge's data to a second card, and the visitor used no card. A physical brute force attack forces or breaks the door or its lock. Skimming captures card data with a hidden reader for later use.

question: Every quarter, the awareness team compares course completion, phishing click rates and the number of suspicious emails reported with earlier quarters, and presents the trend to leadership. Which part of program management is this?
explanation: Recurring reporting and monitoring tracks the same measures at regular intervals and compares them over time to show whether the awareness program is working. Initial reporting records the first baseline at launch, development is the writing of the training content, and execution is the delivery of that training to staff.

question: After malware posing as a PDF reader ran on several kiosks, the team configures them so that only six named programs, identified by their file hashes, are able to start. Which mitigation technique is this?
explanation: An application allow list lets only approved programs run, often identified by hash or signature, and blocks everything else by default, including new malware that no scanner recognizes yet. File integrity monitoring alerts when protected files change, configuration enforcement keeps settings at an approved baseline, and a host-based intrusion prevention system blocks suspicious behavior on one host.

question: Traveling employees reach company applications over an open hotel Wi-Fi network and do not start the VPN client. Which threat does the missing encrypted tunnel expose their sessions to?
explanation: On an open wireless network, anyone nearby can place themselves between a device and the sites it reaches, which is an on-path attack, and a VPN tunnel is what keeps that traffic unreadable. A brute-force attack tries every possible password or key and does not depend on where the user connects. RFID cloning copies a proximity badge. Jamming drowns out the radio signal to deny service, which a VPN does nothing to prevent.

question: Malware copies the authentication cookie from a user's browser, and the attacker reuses it after the user has logged out. The web application still accepts it. Which change would stop this reuse?
options: Requiring a second factor at each sign-in
Ending the session on the server at logout
Encrypting traffic to the application with TLS
Deleting the cookie from the browser at logout
explanation: Ending the session on the server at logout makes its token worthless, so a copied cookie cannot be replayed once the user signs out. Deleting the cookie in the browser leaves the attacker's copy valid, a second factor protects the sign-in that a stolen cookie skips, and TLS protects the cookie in transit but not from malware on the device.

question: A threat profile states that a group has a budget of several million dollars a year and can afford to hire specialists and rent its own servers. Which attribute of a threat actor does the profile describe?
explanation: Resources and funding describe the money, people and equipment that a threat actor can put behind an attack. Level of capability describes skill, that is, how advanced the actor's own techniques are. Internal or external describes whether the actor already holds authorized access, and motive and intent describe why the actor attacks.

question: Endpoints use an internal resolver that blocks known malicious domains and logs every lookup. A review finds that Chrome and Firefox on some laptops send lookups over their own encrypted DNS straight to public resolvers, skipping the internal resolver. Which change closes this gap?
options: Enable DNSSEC validation on the internal resolvers
Turn off DNS over HTTPS in managed browser policy
Block outbound port 53 except from the resolver
Set up split-horizon DNS for internal names
explanation: DNS over HTTPS carries lookups inside ordinary HTTPS traffic on port 443, so turning it off through managed browser policy sends those lookups back to the filtering resolver. Blocking port 53 stops only plain DNS sent around the resolver, DNSSEC validation proves that answers are authentic, and split-horizon DNS gives internal and external clients different answers for the same names.

question: A scan of an internet-facing VPN concentrator shows firmware from 2019 with several published CVEs. The vendor still supports the model and has released corrected firmware, but it was never installed. Which attack surface does this finding describe?
explanation: Software that has a published flaw and an available fix that nobody has applied is vulnerable software, and an internet-facing appliance in that state is an easy target. An unsupported system is one whose vendor no longer issues fixes, which is not the case here. Default credentials are factory passwords left unchanged. Open service ports are listening services that need not be reachable.

question: An analyst wants an alert whenever /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow changes on a Linux server, because an attacker could add a backdoor account by editing them. Which control should be deployed?
explanation: File integrity monitoring records a hash of each critical file at a known-good baseline and alerts when the current hash no longer matches, which reveals edits such as a new account added to /etc/passwd. Log aggregation only collects the logs that systems already write, signature-based anti-malware looks for known malicious code, and data loss prevention watches for sensitive data leaving the organization.

question: A company sends simulated phishing emails to all staff every month and tracks who clicks and who reports each message. What is the PRIMARY purpose of these campaigns?
options: To test whether the mail filter blocks phishing
To train staff to spot and report phishing
To record that staff completed their required training
To see whether attackers could gain a foothold by email
explanation: Recurring phishing simulations exist to train staff to recognize phishing and report it, and to measure that skill over time. Testing the mail filter is a separate technical test, since simulations are normally let past the filter on purpose. Finding out whether an attacker could gain a foothold is the goal of a penetration test, and proof of course completion comes from the training records.

question: Before its new awareness course starts, a company sends one simulated phishing email to every employee and records how many click, so that later results can be compared with that figure. Which stage of the awareness program is this?
explanation: Initial reporting and monitoring records a baseline at the start of a program, so that later measurements can show whether the training is making a difference. Recurring reporting repeats the measurement at intervals after launch, development produces the training content, and execution delivers that training to staff.

question: A company already has a master agreement with a consulting firm. It now wants the firm to migrate its email system, with set deliverables, a schedule and acceptance criteria. Which document should define this project?
explanation: A statement of work (SOW), also called a work order, defines one project's tasks, deliverables, schedule and acceptance criteria under the terms already set by a master service agreement. The master service agreement (MSA) holds the standing legal terms, a service level agreement (SLA) sets ongoing performance targets, and a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) protects confidential information.

question: A penetration tester sends one payroll analyst an email with a tracking attachment. The message appears to come from her manager and mentions her current project, details the tester took from a professional networking site. Which technique is the tester using?
explanation: Spear phishing is phishing aimed at one chosen person and built from research on that person, such as a manager's name and a current project. Whaling is the same approach aimed at a senior executive, which a payroll analyst is not. Brand impersonation copies a known company's name and look. A watering hole attack infects a website the targets already visit instead of sending them a message.

question: A company is moving its password store from unsalted MD5 hashes to salted PBKDF2. The developers cannot compute the new values from the stored hashes, so each account is converted when its user next signs in. Which property of a hash function makes this necessary?
options: It gives an unrelated output for a similar input.
It cannot be reversed to recover the original input.
It cannot give two different outputs for one input.
It gives an output of fixed length for any input.
explanation: A hash function is one-way, so a stored digest cannot be turned back into the password that the new algorithm needs as its input. The other three properties are real but do not block the conversion: a repeatable output is what lets a sign-in be checked, a fixed length keeps every stored value the same size, and an unrelated output for a similar input hides how alike two passwords are.

question: During an intrusion at an insurer, the attacker leaves every system running and changes nothing. The attacker's one action is to copy the policyholder records to a server outside the company, and no message or demand follows. Which motivation does this behavior MOST directly show?
explanation: Data exfiltration is the motivation of an attacker whose aim is to take information out of the organization. Service disruption is ruled out because every system is left running, and philosophical or political beliefs would be shown by a public message. Revenge would need a grievance, and it usually shows itself as damage and not as quiet copying.

question: On the first day of a retailer's annual sale, an attacker floods its online store with traffic so that shoppers cannot place orders. No data is taken, and the attacker sends no message and makes no demand. Which motivation BEST fits this attack?
explanation: Service disruption is the motivation of an attacker whose goal is to stop an organization from serving its customers, which a traffic flood timed for the busiest day achieves. Data exfiltration and espionage both depend on taking information, and no data is taken. Blackmail would come with a threat and a demand, and the attacker makes none.

question: A company moves a batch job from virtual machines it rents from a cloud provider to serverless functions from the same provider. Which security task passes from the company to the provider?
explanation: With serverless functions the provider patches the servers, their operating system and the language runtime, so the operating system work a customer did on rented virtual machines moves to the provider. The host hypervisor was already the provider's responsibility under infrastructure as a service. The company still validates the input its code receives and limits the permissions the job is given.

question: A manager digitally signs a large contract before sending it to a supplier. To create the signature, which item does the signing software process with the manager's signing key?
options: A session key for the supplier
The full text of the contract
explanation: A digital signature is created by hashing the document and then applying the signer's private key to that short hash, not to the whole file. The full text is what a symmetric cipher encrypts to keep a document confidential, a session key is what the recipient's public key protects in hybrid encryption, and a nonce from the other party is what gets signed in challenge-response authentication.

question: Credentials for the domain administrator and root accounts are kept in an encrypted store. An administrator checks one out after MFA, and the store changes the secret when it is returned. Which PAM tool is this?
explanation: Password vaulting keeps privileged account passwords in an encrypted vault, releases one only to an authorized and authenticated user, and can rotate it after use. Just-in-time permissions grant elevated rights for a limited window, multifactor authentication is the sign-in check that guards the vault rather than the vault itself, and access recertification is a periodic review of who holds access.

question: An audit finds that a company still holds former customers' records ten years after the law required it to delete them. Which privacy obligation has the company failed to meet?
explanation: Data retention rules set how long each type of personal data may be kept, and records held past that point must be securely deleted or anonymized. Breach notification concerns reporting security incidents, subject access rights let people obtain a copy of their data, and rectification rights let them have inaccurate data corrected; none of these sets how long data may be kept.

question: A license audit finds six database servers that business units set up themselves. None runs the approved version, has an endpoint agent, or appears in vulnerability scans. Which control would MOST directly have prevented this?
options: A patch tool that enforces the approved version
A procurement process that requires a security review
An annual audit of licenses against installs
A network scan that finds unlisted hosts
explanation: A procurement process that requires security review brings new systems into the inventory, the endpoint agent rollout and the scan schedule before they go live, and systems that bypass it become shadow IT. A license audit and a scan for unlisted hosts find such servers only after they are running, and a patch tool would correct the version but not the missing agent or the missing scans.

question: When HR records an employee's termination, the identity system disables all of that person's accounts and revokes their tokens within minutes. Which identity management practice is this?
explanation: Deprovisioning removes a person's accounts and access as soon as they leave, so that a former employee cannot keep using credentials that should no longer work. Identity proofing confirms who a person is before an account is issued, access attestation is the periodic review in which managers confirm who should keep which access, and single sign-on lets one login reach many applications.

question: An attacker records a company's TLS sessions for a year and then steals the web server's private key. The attacker still cannot decrypt any of the recorded sessions. Which protection explains this?
explanation: Forward secrecy gives every session a key made from a temporary key pair, so a server private key stolen later cannot unlock traffic that was recorded earlier. Certificate pinning makes a client reject an unexpected certificate, mutual authentication makes both ends prove their identity, and certificate revocation only stops the stolen key's certificate from being trusted in new connections.

question: A server is being built to host one internal website. Which step reduces its attack surface before it goes live?
options: Forwarding its logs to a SIEM for central monitoring
Removing the services and accounts that its workload does not need
Scheduling weekly vulnerability scans and reviewing the results
Installing a host-based IDS that alerts on suspicious activity
explanation: Attack surface is the set of ways in, so removing services, open ports and accounts that the server does not need takes away entry points an attacker could use. A host-based IDS and SIEM monitoring detect attacks on whatever remains, and vulnerability scans find weaknesses in it, but none of the three removes anything an attacker can reach.

question: A customer database is valued at $2,000,000. A breach would destroy about 30% of that value, and a breach is expected about once every five years. What is the ALE for this risk?
explanation: The ALE is the single loss expectancy multiplied by the annualized rate of occurrence. Here $2,000,000 times 30% is an SLE of $600,000, and once every five years is an ARO of 0.2, giving $120,000. The figure $600,000 is the SLE alone, $400,000 divides the asset value by five and skips the exposure factor, and $3,000,000 multiplies the SLE by five instead of by 0.2.

question: A tool checks every server each hour against the approved security baseline and automatically reverts any setting that has drifted from it. Which mitigation technique is this?
explanation: Configuration enforcement keeps systems at an approved baseline by checking them on a schedule and correcting any setting that drifts. File integrity monitoring alerts when protected files change, vulnerability scanning looks for known flaws and missing patches, and hardening is the work of choosing and applying secure settings in the first place.

question: A financial institution requires every laptop to prove it has current patches, disk encryption and approved antivirus before it may join the wired or wireless LAN, and sends any laptop that fails to a remediation VLAN. Which solution enforces this?
explanation: Network access control checks a device's posture, such as patch level, encryption and antivirus status, when it tries to connect, and then admits it, blocks it or places it in a remediation VLAN. Port security limits which MAC addresses may use a switch port without checking a device's health, intrusion prevention blocks attacks in traffic, and patch management installs updates without controlling who may connect.

question: During an incident, responders find that the network diagram no longer matches the live topology. Several firewall and switch changes made over the past six months were each approved, tested and applied without an outage. Which step of change management would have prevented the mismatch?
explanation: A change is not complete until the documentation is updated, because diagrams and procedures that lag behind the real configuration mislead the people who depend on them in an incident. A maintenance window limits the effect on users while the work is done. Test results show before release whether the change works. A backout plan restores the previous state when a change fails.

question: A database administrator's own account normally has no administrative rights. When a change request is approved, the PAM system adds the account to the database admin group for two hours and then removes it. Which PAM tool is this?
explanation: Just-in-time permissions give an account elevated rights only for an approved task and remove them when the window closes, so no one holds standing administrator access. Password vaulting stores and releases privileged passwords, session recording captures what an administrator does, and a break-glass account is a sealed emergency login for use when normal access paths fail.

question: A clinic decided that encryption at rest, an addressable specification, was not appropriate for one legacy system, so it left that system unencrypted. What did the HIPAA Security Rule require it to do?
options: Document why and report it to HHS if the risk is high
Document why and adopt an equivalent measure where reasonable
Encrypt it anyway and record the change in its risk analysis
Replace the system and record the plan in its next risk analysis
explanation: An addressable specification is not optional: an entity that finds one not reasonable and appropriate must document why and adopt an equivalent alternative measure where one is reasonable and appropriate. Encrypting anyway is what a required specification would demand, the decision is kept on file for audits and investigations rather than reported to HHS, and replacing the system may be sensible but is not what the rule requires.

question: An outside firm administers a clinic's servers and firewalls under contract. Attackers steal one of that firm's technician accounts and use its remote management tool to install ransomware at the clinic. Which supply chain source was the attackers' way in?
explanation: A firm that runs a customer's systems under contract is a service provider, and its remote access makes it a route into every customer it manages. A hardware provider supplies physical equipment, which was not involved. A software provider writes the programs a customer installs, and the management tool here was abused with a stolen account and was not altered. An identity provider is the system that signs users in.

question: After losing its main data center, an operations team works through a document that says, in order, how to bring up the hot site, restore the databases and redirect users. Which type of document is this?
explanation: A procedure gives ordered, step-by-step instructions for a task, such as failing over to a hot site, while the disaster recovery policy above it requires that recovery be possible. A standard sets specific required values, a policy states intent and assigns authority, and a guideline offers optional advice.

question: A company with twelve branch offices replaces the separate log servers in each branch with one central security monitoring platform. Which benefit does the central design bring?
options: Keeping each branch's logs in the branch
Letting each branch set its own alert rules
Removing any single point of failure
explanation: Central collection puts the events from every branch in one place, so that analysts can correlate them and see an attack that moves from branch to branch. Keeping logs inside each branch and letting each branch set its own alert rules are features of the decentralized design being replaced. The central platform adds a single point of failure rather than removing one, so it needs redundancy of its own.

question: A systems administrator must establish a secure baseline for new Windows workstations and wants a published, widely accepted set of configuration settings to start from. Which resource provides one?
explanation: A CIS Benchmark is a published, consensus-based list of secure configuration settings for a specific product, which makes it a ready starting point for a baseline. CVSS base scores rate how severe a vulnerability is, CVE records identify individual known vulnerabilities, and MITRE ATT&CK techniques describe how attackers behave. None of the three says how a workstation should be configured.

question: While cleaning up after a malware outbreak, the IT team puts four measures in place. Which of them is a detective control?
options: Application allow listing on each workstation
A login banner warning that systems are monitored
Re-imaging infected hosts from a known-good baseline image
File integrity monitoring that alerts on changed system files
explanation: A detective control identifies and records an attack or a change, and file integrity monitoring does this by alerting when protected system files are altered. Re-imaging infected hosts is corrective, because it restores them after the outbreak, application allow listing is preventive, because it stops unapproved programs from running, and a monitoring banner is a deterrent.

question: A managed security provider watches a company's SIEM around the clock. After a breach, the company learns that the provider took three days to escalate a high-severity alert. Which agreement should have set specific response and escalation times?
explanation: A service level agreement (SLA) sets measurable performance commitments, such as how quickly alerts must be triaged and escalated, and the remedies when they are missed. A master service agreement (MSA) holds the overall legal terms of the relationship, a memorandum of understanding (MOU) records nonbinding intent, and a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) protects confidential information.

question: Ana must send Marco a contract that only he can read, and he must be able to prove to a court that it came from her unchanged. The two have exchanged certificates but share no secret key. Which keys does Ana use?
options: Her private key to encrypt, her private key to sign
Marco's public key to encrypt, her private key to sign
Marco's public key to encrypt, her public key to sign
Her private key to encrypt, her public key to sign
explanation: Encrypting with the recipient's public key means that only the recipient's private key can open the message, and signing with the sender's private key lets anyone confirm the origin with the sender's public key. A signature made with a public key proves nothing, because anyone can hold that key. Encrypting with the sender's own private key hides nothing, because anyone with her public key can reverse it.

question: A popular browser extension is sold to a new developer, who publishes a version that reports every site its users visit to an outside server. Browsers install that version automatically from the official store. Which type of vulnerability does this show?
explanation: A malicious update delivers harmful code through a product's normal update channel, so users who trust that channel install it without any warning. Side loading means installing software from outside the official store, which did not happen here. A zero-day is an unknown flaw that attackers exploit before a fix exists, while this version was built to collect data on purpose, and a misconfiguration is an insecure setting chosen by a system's owner.

question: A flaw is found on a server that the business cannot operate without. Which part of a CVSS score lets the organization raise the flaw's rating to reflect how much that server matters to it?
explanation: The CVSS security requirement metrics (confidentiality, integrity and availability requirements) let an organization weight a score by how much the affected asset matters to it. Modified attack vector adjusts how the flaw can be reached in the organization's own network, confidentiality impact is a base metric for how much data the flaw itself exposes, and exploit code maturity reflects whether working exploit code exists.

question: A company hires an accounting firm that has no other ties to it to examine its controls and give its shareholders an independent opinion. Which type of audit is this?
explanation: An external audit is carried out by an independent outside firm, which gives its opinion weight with shareholders, lenders and customers. An internal audit is done by the company's own audit staff, a regulatory audit is carried out by a government agency that enforces a law, and a customer audit is one that a client performs under its contract.

question: What distinguishes a continuous risk assessment from a recurring one?
options: It starts when a specific event occurs
It covers a single project and then ends
It repeats on a fixed calendar schedule
It updates whenever new data comes in
explanation: A continuous risk assessment runs all the time, usually through automated tools such as scanners and a SIEM, so its results change as soon as new data arrives. A fixed calendar schedule marks a recurring assessment, a start prompted by a specific event marks an ad hoc one, and coverage of a single project that then ends marks a one-time assessment.

question: Analysts investigating a break-in at a defense contractor conclude that it was the work of an advanced persistent threat. Which finding would BEST support that conclusion?
options: Ransom notes left on file servers
explanation: An advanced persistent threat is defined by staying inside a chosen target, unnoticed, for a long time while it works toward a specific goal such as stealing designs. Ransom notes point to a criminal group that wants payment, and public claims of responsibility point to a hacktivist. Well-known exploits run unchanged point to an unskilled attacker.

question: A security policy requires every encryption key to be replaced on a fixed schedule and the old key to be destroyed after a transition period. Which risk does this practice reduce?
options: A lost key leaves the encrypted data unreadable.
A stolen key keeps exposing data for a long time.
A key derived from a passphrase is easily guessed.
A public key is tied to the wrong identity.
explanation: Key rotation limits how long a stolen key stays useful, because data protected after the change needs a key that the thief does not hold. A lost key is covered by key escrow or backup, a key that is easily guessed from a passphrase is countered by key stretching, and a public key tied to the wrong identity is the problem that certificates from a trusted CA solve.

question: A company wants its firewall to block Tor, which can use port 443 and resemble ordinary HTTPS, while still allowing normal web browsing. Which firewall capability makes this possible?
explanation: Application-layer filtering identifies the application inside a connection from the content and pattern of its traffic rather than from its port, so a next-generation firewall can block Tor while allowing other HTTPS. Stateful inspection only tracks whether packets belong to an allowed connection, port-based lists cannot tell two applications on port 443 apart, and MAC address filtering controls which devices may use a local segment.

question: Each time a Windows server boots, it runs an encoded PowerShell command. No Run key, startup folder, service or scheduled task starts it, and the only trace is a new entry in the repository under C:\Windows\System32\wbem. Which persistence mechanism is this?
explanation: A WMI event subscription stores a trigger, such as system startup, and a command in the WMI repository under System32\wbem, so it survives reboots without touching the usual autostart locations. A GPO startup script is defined in a Group Policy object, a boot sector rootkit loads before Windows does, and a hijacked DLL is a planted library that a legitimate program loads in place of the real one.

question: A scan finds four confirmed flaws: CVSS 9.1 on an isolated lab server with no sensitive data, 8.4 on an internal print server, 7.8 on the internet-facing payment server and 6.9 on the public marketing site. Which should be remediated FIRST?
explanation: A CVSS base score rates a flaw in isolation, so risk-based prioritization also weighs how exposed the affected system is and how sensitive its data is. The payment server faces the internet and handles card data, which puts its 7.8 flaw ahead of a 9.1 on an isolated lab server with nothing sensitive, an 8.4 on an internal print server and a 6.9 on a public site that holds nothing confidential.

question: Which decoy deployed by a security team is a honeypot?
options: A decoy password that alerts the team when it is used
A decoy file that alerts the team when it is opened
A decoy network that alerts the team when it is probed
A decoy server that alerts the team when it is attacked
explanation: A honeypot is a single decoy system, such as a server, that draws intruders away from production systems so that defenders can watch what they do. A honeynet is a whole decoy network of such systems, a honeyfile is a bait file, and a honeytoken is a bait item of data such as a false password.

question: When an employee clicks the link in a simulated phishing email, a short lesson opens at once and points out the clues they missed. What is the main benefit of showing the lesson at that point?
options: It matches the lesson to each person's job
It comes when the mistake is still fresh
It shows staff the newest attacks seen by the company
It gives a baseline for judging later campaigns
explanation: Training given at the moment of a mistake, often called just-in-time training, works because the lesson arrives while the error is still fresh in the person's mind. Matching lessons to each job is the benefit of role-based training, a baseline for judging later campaigns comes from the first measurement, and lessons on the newest attacks come from keeping the content up to date.

question: A man who closed his account with an EU online store asks the store to erase every record it keeps about him. Which GDPR right is he exercising?
explanation: The right to be forgotten, formally the right to erasure, lets a person have their personal data deleted when, for example, it is no longer needed for the purpose it was collected for. The right of access gives a copy of the data, the right to object stops certain processing such as direct marketing, and the right to portability lets a person move the data they supplied to another provider.

question: Laptops issued to employees who left six months ago were never collected. Their drives are encrypted, but each laptop still holds a valid VPN certificate. Which risk does this PRIMARILY create?
options: Disclosure of data to a later buyer
Remote access to the internal network
Tampered firmware from the supply chain
Unlicensed use of the company's software
explanation: A laptop that still holds a valid VPN certificate can still connect to the company network, so an unreturned device gives its former user, or anyone who obtains it, a way into internal systems. Encryption protects the files from a later buyer, unlicensed use is a compliance matter rather than a path into the network, and tampered firmware is a supply chain risk for new equipment. Recovering devices and revoking their certificates at offboarding closes the gap.

question: A threat actor registers an application with a familiar name and emails employees a link to their identity provider's genuine permission page. Several click Allow, and none of them types a password. What does the threat actor now hold that lets it read their mail?
options: A password hash captured from the sign-in
An access token issued to the third-party app
A one-time code relayed from the phone
A session cookie copied from the browser
explanation: Consent phishing tricks a user into approving a malicious application, and the identity provider then issues that application an access token for the user's data. No password hash is captured, because nobody types a password. A session cookie is what session hijacking steals from a browser. A one-time code is what an attacker relays in a real-time attack on multifactor authentication. The remedy is to revoke the application's approval, since no password was stolen.

question: Once a ransomware incident is closed, the incident team meets for its lessons learned review. Which task belongs in this meeting?
options: Choosing the order for restoring the servers
Confirming that the backdoor accounts are gone
Agreeing on changes to the response plan
Deciding which hosts to cut off from the network
explanation: The lessons learned review looks back at how the incident was handled and turns what went wrong into agreed changes to the plan, the playbooks and the controls. Choosing the order of restoration belongs to recovery, deciding which hosts to cut off belongs to containment, and confirming that backdoor accounts are gone is part of eradication, all of which are finished before the incident is closed.

question: Employees are told not to plug any USB drive or charging cable of unknown origin into a work laptop, and to hand any drive they find to the IT department. Which training topic does this instruction belong to?
explanation: Removable media training warns that a found or unknown USB drive or cable can carry malware that runs as soon as it is connected, so such items go to IT unused. Password management covers creating and protecting passwords, operational security covers keeping sensitive details private, and situational awareness covers noticing suspicious people and objects nearby.

question: A company moves its CISO from reporting to the CIO to reporting to the board's risk committee. What does this change mainly achieve?
options: Tighter control of security spending by finance
Independence from the IT operations it oversees
A sharper focus on legal and regulatory obligations
Closer alignment with day-to-day IT projects
explanation: Moving the CISO's reporting line away from the CIO keeps security oversight independent of the IT operations it judges, so risks reach the board without being filtered by the people who run those systems. Reporting to the CIO brings closer alignment with IT projects, reporting to the CFO ties security spending to finance, and reporting to general counsel sharpens the focus on legal and regulatory duties.

question: Once the contract is signed, a company checks its cloud provider's uptime, incident response times and patching against the agreed terms each month, and reviews the provider's security reports every quarter. What is this practice called?
explanation: Vendor monitoring is the ongoing review of a vendor's performance and security against the contract after it is signed, through metrics, reports and periodic reassessment. Due diligence is the checking done before signing, questionnaires gather a vendor's written answers at one point in time, and penetration testing simulates an attack on the vendor's systems.

question: A company wants the SSH, SNMP and syslog traffic of its routers and switches to travel on links that carry no user traffic, so that a compromised workstation has no route to any device's management interface. Which design achieves this?
options: An out-of-band network for management traffic
A jump server that brokers admin sessions
TLS encryption for the management protocols
explanation: An out-of-band management network gives device management interfaces their own separate path, so SSH, SNMP and syslog never share links or addresses that a compromised workstation can reach. A jump server controls and records administrator sessions, TLS protects management traffic from being read, and multifactor authentication protects logins, but with each of them the management traffic still travels on the links that carry user traffic.

question: A password reset link carries a token that is only the Base64 encoding of the username and the time of the request. A tester builds a working link for another account without ever seeing that account's email. Which weakness does this show?
options: A session token set before login
A reset token made from guessable values
A session cookie open to script access
A reset link with no expiry time
explanation: A reset token must be a long random value that cannot be worked out from anything an attacker knows, and Base64 is only an encoding that anyone can reproduce. A link that never expires and a session token set before login (session fixation) are different flaws, since this tester forged a fresh link without capturing anything. A cookie that scripts can read matters only when an attacker can run a script in the victim's browser.

question: A company contracts for a warm site to use if its data center is lost. What will that site offer when a disaster is declared?
options: Portable servers that are trucked in on demand
Powered rooms that need servers installed first
Installed servers that need recent data restored
Running servers that already hold current data
explanation: A warm site has servers and network links already installed, but recent backups must be restored onto them before it takes over, so recovery takes hours to days. Running servers that already hold current data describe a hot site, powered rooms waiting for servers describe a cold site, and portable servers trucked in on demand describe a mobile site.

question: An IDS raises alerts for a port scan from an internal IP address. The company's vulnerability management team runs network scans every week from its own servers. What should the analyst do FIRST?
options: Escalate the alerts to the incident response manager
Check whether the address belongs to an approved scanner
Move the device at that address to a quarantine VLAN
Capture a memory image from the device at that address
explanation: Internal port scans are often run by approved vulnerability scanners, so the first step is to confirm whether the source is one of them before treating the activity as an attack. Quarantining the device, capturing its memory and escalating to the incident response manager are the right moves once the scan is confirmed as unauthorized, but taken first they can disrupt a sanctioned tool and waste effort.

question: A company's clients learn of revoked certificates from a signed list that the CA publishes once a day. The security team wants each client to check a certificate's current status at the moment the certificate is presented. Which should the team implement?
explanation: OCSP lets a client ask a responder for the current status of one certificate, so a revocation takes effect without waiting for the next published list. A CRL is that periodically published list, a CSR is the request an applicant sends to obtain a certificate, and an RA is the registration authority that checks an applicant's identity before the CA issues one.

question: A company discovers that a chip soldered onto the circuit boards of its new network switches during assembly contains a hidden backdoor. Which part of the supply chain introduced this threat?
explanation: A component altered during manufacturing is a hardware supply chain compromise, so the device is malicious before it ever reaches the buyer. Here the hardware manufacturer, or one of its own suppliers, introduced the threat. A software supplier introduces threats through tainted code or updates, a managed service provider through abuse of its remote access to clients, and the logistics carrier's stage is where devices can be intercepted and altered in transit.

question: A company sets a recovery time objective (RTO) of two hours for its order system. What do the two hours measure?
options: The window of recent data allowed to be lost
The time allowed to restore service
The average time a repair actually takes
The total downtime allowed in a year
explanation: A recovery time objective is the longest a service may stay down after a disruption, so a two-hour RTO means it must be back in service within two hours. The window of data that may be lost is the recovery point objective, the average time a repair takes is the mean time to repair, and an annual downtime allowance is an availability target, often written into an SLA.

question: At a bank, a wire transfer entered by one employee must be approved by a different employee before it is sent. Which risk does this rule mainly address?
options: An insider completing a fraudulent payment
Malware moving from office PCs to payment servers
A clerk keeping rights from a past role
explanation: Separation of duties splits a sensitive task between people, so that fraud by one insider needs a second person to collude and an honest mistake gets a second look. Segmentation keeps malware on office computers away from payment systems, encryption stops an outsider from reading intercepted transfer details, and periodic access reviews remove rights left over from a past role.

question: A CISO estimates that a breach of the ERP system would cost $2.5 million and has a 10% chance of happening in any year. A proposed control would cost $300,000 a year. What should the CISO advise the board?
options: Approve it, because the ALE is $2.5 million a year
Decline it, because the ALE is $250,000 a year
Decline it, because the SLE is $250,000
Approve it, because the SLE is $2.5 million
explanation: A control is worth funding when its yearly cost is less than the drop in ALE it brings. Even removing this risk's whole ALE of $250,000 ($2.5 million times 10%) would not cover a $300,000 yearly cost. The $2.5 million figure is the SLE, the cost of one breach, so it is neither the ALE nor the right figure to weigh a yearly cost against, and $250,000 is the ALE rather than the SLE.

question: A company runs every workload on one cloud provider. A risk assessment flags two concerns: being locked in to that provider and losing service if the provider suffers a widespread outage. Which strategy addresses both concerns?
options: Negotiating a stronger SLA with the provider
Running workloads across two or more providers
Running workloads in two regions of the same provider
Keeping backup copies with a second provider
explanation: A multi-cloud strategy runs workloads on more than one provider, so an outage at one provider does not stop service and moving away from any single provider stays practical. Two regions of the same provider survive a regional outage but not a provider-wide one or lock-in, a stronger SLA pays credits without restoring service, and backups at a second provider keep the data safe but leave the workloads down.

question: After firewalls, IDS and endpoint protection are in place, an analyst rates the chance of a successful breach at 5% a year, and management signs off on that level in the risk register. What does the 5% figure describe?
explanation: Residual risk is the risk that remains after controls are applied, and it is what management formally accepts once it falls within appetite. Inherent risk is the level before any controls, risk appetite is the overall amount of risk the organization is willing to take on, and a risk threshold is the level that triggers escalation.

question: A tester overflows a stack buffer in a Windows program, overwrites the return address and jumps to injected code, which is found in the same position each time the program starts. The program was built without ASLR. How would ASLR have hindered this exploit?
options: It checks a guard value before a function returns
It places memory regions at random locations
It marks stack memory as non-executable
It verifies the program signature before launch
explanation: Address space layout randomization places the stack, heap and libraries at different locations each time a program starts, so an attacker cannot know in advance where to send execution. Marking the stack as non-executable is data execution prevention, and checking a guard value before a function returns is a stack canary. Verifying a signature before launch is code signing, which detects a tampered program file rather than a memory attack.

question: A company has 200 low-risk suppliers and wants a consistent, low-cost first look at each one's security practices before deciding which ones need a closer review. Which assessment method fits this purpose BEST?
explanation: Questionnaires collect each vendor's written answers about its controls in a standard format, which makes them a cheap and consistent first screen across many suppliers, with deeper review saved for those that raise concerns. On-site audits and penetration testing cost far more time and money per supplier, and supply chain analysis traces where a product's parts come from rather than surveying security practices.

question: On a payroll clerk's computer, an analyst finds a hidden file that grows whenever the clerk types. It holds every user name, password and card number exactly as it was entered, and it is sent to an outside address each night. Which type of malware is present?
explanation: A keylogger records what is typed, which is why the file holds credentials and card numbers exactly as they were entered. A rootkit is identified by what it hides from the operating system's own tools, not by what it collects. A Trojan is identified by its disguise as a useful program, and nothing here shows one. A worm is identified by spreading to other computers by itself.

question: An attacker is using a stolen service account on three servers. Some responders want to disable the account at once, and others want to watch for a few days to learn the attacker's tools and targets. What is the main risk of waiting?
options: The chance to study the attacker's tools is lost
The attacker learns that they have been found
The attacker takes data or reaches more systems
The business service that uses the account stops
explanation: Delaying containment to gather intelligence leaves the attacker free to act, so the main risk of watching is that data is stolen or the compromise spreads while the team observes. Tipping off the attacker, losing the chance to study their tools and stopping the service that runs under the account are all costs of acting at once, which is why the choice is a deliberate risk decision for management.

question: A company issues smartphones and tablets to its field staff. It must enforce storage encryption and a screen lock on each one, and it must be able to erase one that is lost. Which solution provides these controls?
explanation: Mobile device management (MDM) pushes configuration policy to phones and tablets, including required encryption and screen locks, and it can wipe a lost device remotely. Network access control decides whether a device may join the network but does not configure it.
